extractor.note: Whole file grep-counted for the theme's search terms plus 'eidetic', 'eidos', 'Wesensschau', 'free variation', 'immutable', 'innate', 'residuum' and 'Descartes'. 'eidetic' and 'eidos' occur once each, both in the Concluding Word; 'Wesensschau', 'free variation', 'immutable', 'innate' and 'residuum' occur nowhere; 'Descartes' occurs six times, all about the Meditations as a method of radical grounding. Closely read the Introduction (lines 11-78) and the Concluding Word (855-859).

coverage_note: Covers the Introduction and the Concluding Word. Parts I and II, the Appendices, and § 93 (whose heading names Descartes but whose body is empty in this commentary) were keyword-scanned only. The theme's 61 sections of hits in this file are overwhelmingly 'essential' used adverbially or in the phrases 'essential necessity' and 'essential generality'; the eidetic vocabulary proper appears only at the very end.

units.claim: Logic in the genuine sense is traced to the Platonic founding, as a site for investigating the essential requirements of genuine knowing and genuine science.
units.quote: logic conceived as a site for investigating the essential requirements of "genuine" knowing and "genuine" science

units.claim: Logic's great function is said to be investigating in essential generality the paths to ultimate principles, and so unfolding the essence of genuine science as such, its pure possibility.
units.quote: through unfolding the essence of genuine science as such (its pure possibility), to give actual science norm and guidance

units.claim: Logic is charged with going astray from its own sense by failing to pursue the pure essential norms of science according to all its essential formations.
units.quote: Instead of pursuing the pure essential norms of science according to all its essential formations

units.claim: Formal logic is called the first historical attempt at a universal science-theory, a theory related to the essential conditions of possible science as such.
units.quote: a theory related to the essential conditions of possible science as such

units.claim: A purely possible world in general is said to arise as eidos concretely through the method of eidetic variation from the factually given world.
units.quote: which as eidos must concretely arise through the method of eidetic variation from the factually given world

units.claim: A transcendental aesthetic in a new sense is projected as the eidetic description of the universal a priori without which objects could not unitarily appear before the categorial actions.
units.quote: the eidetic description of the universal a priori without which in mere experience and before the categorial actions, objects could not unitarily appear

absences.expected_because: The Introduction runs the whole Cartesian theme - the Discourse on Method, the Meditations as first philosophy, the failure of Descartes' own radical grounding - and so is where Descartes' doctrine of essences would be taken up if this commentary took it up; it engages only his method.
absences.note: Bears on gap-007. Descartes is named repeatedly in this section, which is why the absence is informative: the engagement is with the Meditations as a programme of radical grounding, never with vera et immutabilis natura.

absences.expected_because: This is the only place in the commentary where eidos and eidetic variation appear, and it projects a transcendental aesthetic as eidetic description of the world-a-priori - the natural place to say what an essence so obtained is, in residuum or immutability terms.
absences.note: The eidos here is obtained by variation from the factually given world; nothing is said of innateness, immutability, or a residuum.
